A report revealed that documents and application data of candidates in a public competition run by a Naples hospital, including health data, were accessible online through a platform managed by an outsourced supplier. The Garante found the hospital had not given candidates proper privacy information, had no Article 28 contract with the supplier, lacked a lawful basis for disseminating the data, and had failed to ensure adequate security. The data stayed online for about 25 days and affected over 2000 candidates. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and ordered the hospital to pay a fine of EUR 80,000, with publication of the decision.

Scanshare s.r.l., an IT outsourcer running the online application portal for a hospital's public recruitment competition, left folders with candidates' documents, including health data, publicly accessible for about 25 days after a maintenance intervention. The Garante found that the company acted without an Article 28 appointment or any legal basis, and that its security measures were inadequate (including sending data on an unprotected CD). It declared the data unusable, restricted all further processing of the candidates' data, ordered the company to report back within 30 days, and fined it EUR 60,000. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.
Spanish DPA (AEPD) held that companies must respect the right to access and provide information when a citizen demands it in line with Article 15 GDPR.

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernrådet) overturned the Norwegian DPA's (Datatilsynet) decision to reprimand a local missionary organization's use of private camera surveillance footage under Article (6)(1)(f).
The Spanish DPA fined a neighbourhood community EUR 10.000 for infringing Article 5(1)(f) of the GDPR.

This is the Inspectorate's decision on two appeals (one from the company, one from the data subject) against its own decision of 30 July 2020. The original decision fined the company EUR 6,250 under Article 83(5)(a) GDPR. The company, without a legal basis, had emailed its employees the name and tuberculosis diagnosis of an infected colleague, before the health authority had given any instruction. The Inspectorate rejected the procedural objections and the company's claimed legal bases (Art. 6(1)(d), 9(2)(e) and (i)). It found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation and integrity/confidentiality. It rejected the data subject's argument that the fine was too low and the company's argument that it was too high or the breach minor, and left the original decision and fine unchanged.

The Italian DPA has acknowledged the deferral of the deadline for joining the IT system to make available electronic invoices for VAT operators and their customers, as proposed by the Italian Revenue Agency to March, 1st 2021.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) provides a non-binding opinion on the legal basis for sending an SMS message to all users about a new application by the Slovenian National Institute of Public Health (NIJZ). The IP found that there was no legal basis for the SMS by relying on Articles 148 and 158 of the Slovenian law transposing the ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC .

The Icelandic Data Protection Authority (Persónuvernd) held *that Creditinfo Lánstrausti (an Icelandic credit agency) is allowed to process a data subject's personal data from the Icelandic debtors' default register and information on a company owned by the data subject for the calculation of a credit score but *that Creditinfo Lánstrausti is prohibited from processing information on searches in the debtor's default register regarding the data subject and information from the tax register.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) held that an environmental regulation enforcement agency violated Article 5 and 6 GDPR by disclosing the name of a complainant's flatmate, and their familial relationships in a decision addressed towards the complainant for littering.

The Austrian DPA held that the right to access under Article 15(1)(h) GDPR applies to all kinds of profiling rather than only to automated decision making under Article 22(1) and (4) GDPR. The DPA further rejected the controller's argument that protection of a trade secret should form an exception to the complainants' right to access. tbd

A company that recruits job candidates contacted a person via LinkedIn in July 2019 and kept his data without any legal basis. After he asked for erasure on 30 March 2020 and was told the data had been deleted, the company still sent him commercial emails in July and August 2020. The Czech authority issued a penalty order finding a breach of Article 6(1) and of the right to erasure under Article 17(1). It imposed a single fine of CZK 50,000, applying the absorption principle, with the unlawful processing as the more serious offence.
The Romanian DPA fined a data controller €2000 for transmitting the login data of 1300 data subjects to incorrect email addresses.

In a case at the intersection of telecommunications law and data protection, the Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernrådet) upheld the Norwegian DPA's (Datatilsynet) request for information to OpenX.
The Belgian DPA (APB/GBA) imposed a fine of € 5000 to a politician for sending unsolicited political email to the plaintiff, violating among others the purpose limitation principle.

The HDPA of Greece examined the complaint for the violation of GDPR against the Greek Ministry of Education and Religion of a parent who had filed a request in order for their son to be exempted from the participation in the religious education course and generally from any religious activity at their high school, due to religious conscience related reasons. The parent's request was rejected and they had to provide the school with an additional form underlining the fact that their son was not Orthodox Christian, but their request was again rejected this time as overdue. Τhe parent's additional request for the school to erase their son's personal data pertaining to his religious beliefs was also rejected, while the complainant also complained about the issue of the inscription on school leaving certificates of the conduct of the respective student.

An employee had submitted a complaint to the Greek Data Protection Authority about the video surveillance in the store in which she had worked. The Greek DPA held that a CCTV system shall be handled as subject to Article 4(1) and Article 4(2) of GDPR Regulation. That judgment does not mean that any CCTV surveillance in workplaces and under any circumstances is forbidden; the Data Protection Officer seems to make an obiter dictum legal comment and not a ratio decidendi of that decision. The Greek Office, before finishing, its his judgment, goes through the principle of proportionality and finds, that in these facts, the merchant had not violated employees' rights when he installed the surveillance system.

UK DPA (Information Commissioner’s Office - ICO) issues £130.000 fine for serious contravention to Privacy and E-Communications Regulations (EC Directive) 2003 (PECR) by making unsolicited calls for the purposes of direct marketing in relation to occupational or personal pension schemes.

The Icelandic DPA (Personuvernd) established that by granting access to the complainant's online banking account to an unauthorised person, Íslandsbanki (bank) was processing personal data in violation of Articles 8(1)(6), 23, 24, and 27 Act 90/2018 (Articles 5(1)(f), 24, 25 and 32 GDPR).

The Garante received a complaint that the municipality of Casaloldo had published on its website, in the 'Amministrazione trasparente' section, a determination and attached documents from a public recruitment competition. These documents showed names, identification data and intermediate test scores of about 50 candidates, including the complainant, who was not admitted to the oral test. The Garante found that the publication had no legal basis under the Italian Data Protection Code (Art. 2-ter) and breached the GDPR principles and Article 6. The municipality removed the documents, and the Garante imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.
Spanish DPA held that the sending of the electoral roll by e-mail to different persons outside and inside the company constitutes an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

The Austrian Data Protection Authority (DSB) rejected a complaint on data erasure because the respondent was a media company processing data for journalistic purposes. The DSB considered itself not competent to handle such a complaint under § 9 of the Austrian Data Protection Act and Article 85 GDPR.

Datatilsynet holds that the Norwegian Customs Authority processed personal data from the Automatic Numberplate Recognition (ANPR) database without a legal basis, as it processed data not that was not connected to cross-border traffic. The case was decided under the national implementation of 95/46/EC.
The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) fined an apartment building owners association €500 for illegally processing the image of a data subject.

A company failed to respond to a data subject's access request of 11 November 2019 made through a law firm. The company stayed silent even after the Authority warned it in March 2020. The Authority first issued a penalty order of CZK 50,000; the company objected, so ordinary proceedings continued. It found a violation of Article 15(1) GDPR, imposed a fine of CZK 30,000 and costs of CZK 1,000. The fine was set at the very low end of the range, with the complex old credit fraud case counted as mitigating.

A company sent unsolicited offers to owners of industrial property rights, using personal data taken from public patent registers. One owner objected by email on 9 July 2020 and asked for erasure, but the company never replied. The Czech DPA, by a penalty order (příkaz), found it had infringed Article 12(3) GDPR by not informing the data subject of action taken within one month. It fined the company CZK 50,000, near the bottom of the range.

A former customer complained that Bankia still held his personal data 16 years after he stopped being a client. Bankia argued the data were blocked, but the AEPD found they were still accessible to branch staff and that the bank had not updated its retention policy until March 2020. The AEPD's proposed resolution found a breach of Article 5(1)(b) GDPR and proposed a EUR 50,000 fine. Bankia paid EUR 40,000 on 20 August 2020, using the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, so the proceeding was closed.

The ICO rules that there is sufficient legitimate interest in disclosure of the information relating to the job description of the CCG officers commissioning health care and it outweighs the data subjects’ fundamental rights and freedoms.
The Icelandic DPA held that an employer did not lawfully process the fingerprint data of its employees for the purpose of logging in and out the employees in the company's payroll system.

The Icelandic Data Protection Authority (Persónuvernd) held that the publication of an individual's personal information about another person on their Facebook page occurred in breach of Article 6 GDPR.

The Icelandic Data Protection Authority (Persónuvernd) held that the publication of an individual's personal information (address) about another person on their Facebook page occurred in breach of Article 6 GDPR.
The AEPD fined a basketball federation €3000 for disseminating personal data without consent.

The HDPA of Greece examined a complaint of four data subjects (namely, the two owners of the property, a Private Company [P.C.] - renter of the property for the purposes of completing the ongoing on-site construction work , and the legal representative of said company) against a data processor regarding the violation of their right to protect their personal data and of their privacy. The case revolved around the latter person’s action of installing and making use of a video surveillance system including two cameras within their own property, but whose area of surveillance included the complainants’ property and public street. The HDPA, after addressing the meaning of the data processing principles (Article 5 GDPR) and the details of data processing via video surveillance, it made use of its corrective powers (Article 58(2) GDPR) in order for the violation of Article 5 GDPR to be restored, as well as of its authority to impose an administrative fine that amounted to 8,000 EUR.

The Slovenian data protection authority (Information Commissioner) gave its non-binding opinion on the data protection roles under Article 4(7) and (8) GDPR of the entities involved in clinical trials in Slovenia , holding that a case-by-case analysis per processing operation is neccessary.

The Polish DPA inspected the Surveyor General, which publishes land and building register data, including land and mortgage register numbers, on the Geoportal2 website for counties lacking their own infrastructure. The Surveyor General obstructed the inspection and disputed that it was the controller. The DPA found that publishing the land and mortgage register numbers had no legal basis, infringing Art. 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR. It ordered the publication to stop within 14 days and imposed the maximum fine of PLN 100,000 for a public body. The remaining issues, the record of processing under Art. 30, had been fixed during the proceedings, so that part was discontinued.

In a non-binding opinion, the Slovenian data protection authority (Information Commissioner) held that employers are not permitted to process employees' personal data to monitor their compliance with imposed quarantine.

The Spanish DPA fined a gas installation company €3000 for violating Article 6(1)(a) GDPR, as it stored the personal data of its customers in a notebook without having a legal basis to do so, and did not inform its data subjects of this data processing.

The Spanish DPA held that sending an e-mail without using the BCC (Blind Carbon Copy) option is an infringement of Article 5(1)(b) and (f) GDPR. In particular, the sharing of the complainant's e-mail address with third parties without the owner's prior consent is unlawful.

The Norwegian DPA (Datatilsynet) issued a reprimand to a Norwegian pension fund (Bodø Kommunale Pensjonskasse - BKP) for unnecessarily processing and transferring data in violation of Article 6 and 9 GDPR.
The Polish DPA fined the Warsaw University of Life Sciences (SGGW) with PLN 50000 as a result of a data breach that exposed over 80000 records about study candidates from the last 5 years.

A member of the public found hardcopy documents holding patients' personal data in a public recycling facility and told the HSE, which reported the breach to the Irish DPC. The DPC decided on 18 August 2020 that the hospital/HSE had infringed Articles 5 and 32 GDPR by not applying appropriate security measures to the use and disposal of paper records. It imposed an administrative fine of €65,000, a reprimand and an order to bring its processing and disposal systems into compliance. The hospital accepted the findings and the ruling was not appealed.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) held that a data subject's request for information about which of their employees looked up their personal information in a police office case file system could be refused.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) ruled that a credit agency (Creditinfo) is permitted to use information on the complainant's previous entries in the default register when preparing reports on the complainant's credit rating.

The DPA found that a controller did not have to comply with the data subject's request to erase personal data relating to the recruitment process, as it was necessary to store data for up to 2 years in order for the controller to defend itself against possible discrimination claims.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into Tusla, the child and family agency, following numerous personal data breach notifications. It found that Tusla infringed Article 32(1) GDPR through inadequate security in several processing operations (the NCCIS case management system, internal and external transmission of data, printing and scanning) and also infringed Article 33(1) on breach notification. It issued a reprimand and an order, and imposed two administrative fines: EUR 50,000 for the NCCIS infringement and EUR 35,000 for printing and scanning, totalling EUR 85,000. Mitigating factors such as cooperation and earlier fines substantially reduced the amounts.

This is the AEPD's decision on an appeal for reconsideration (recurso de reposición) filed by Orange Espagne against its sanctioning decision PS/00452/2019 of 23 June 2020. Following a complaint, Orange was found to have processed the complainant's personal data to register six telephone lines he said were fraudulently contracted, and to have included him in the Asnef credit-information file, without a lawful basis under Article 6.1 GDPR. The AEPD had imposed a EUR 80,000 fine for this very serious infringement. In this decision the appeal is dismissed and the fine stands, as the appeal raised no new facts or legal arguments.

The Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA) ordered the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to comply with its recommendations regarding the security issues it identified in the Visa Information System (VIS).

The Spanish DPA has fined "ASOCIACIÓN DE VIGILANTES DE SEGURIDAD DEL AEROPUERTO DE BARCELONA" with €1800 for an infringement of the principle of confidentiality in the processing of data, as set out in article 5 GDPR.
The Cypriot DPA (Commissioner) asked the company KEO PLC to suspend its new employee time tracking system, due to a lack of compatibility with Article 7(4) and Article 35(9) of GDPR.

No fine. The Danish DPA reported PrivatBo A.M.B.A. af 1993 to the police on 4 August 2020 and recommended DKK 150,000. The police closed the case by mistake and it cannot be reopened, so on 2 May 2022 the DPA issued serious criticism instead. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

A customer ordered goods and received an invoice from the company, then asked it in writing for access to her personal data under Article 15 GDPR. The company never answered; the letter came back undelivered, and it also ignored the Office's warning and requests for comment. After an inspection, the Office issued a penalty order finding the company committed a misdemeanour by breaching the right of access. It imposed a fine of CZK 50,000, set near the lower end of the range.

The HPDA of Greece imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 on a candidate of the June 2019 Greek parliamentary elections due to the violation - via the candidate's pre-election manually operated phone calls-made campaign - of the data subject's right to access their data (Article 15 GDPR) and the violation of Article 11(2) Law 3471/2006 that concerns the protection of personal data in the sector of electronic communications and, more especially, the "opt-out" system regarding manually operated phone calls for promotional purposes.

The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) held that the "data management prospectus" of a controller did not meet the standards required by the GDPR, and ordered the controller to bring its policy in line with Articles 12 and 13 GDPR.

The HDPA of Greece examined the complaint of an employee of the Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator S.A. against the latter regarding a possible violation of the data subject's right to access their data (Article 15 GDPR) via the refusal to issue a certificate of employment status needed by the complainant for the purposes of fulfilling the prerequisites for a new position they were chosen for. The HDPA held that the subject-matter of the complaint was no longer existent, but referred the case to the HDPA Plenary for the purposes of defining the relation between the data subject's right to access their data and the issuing of certificates of employment.

ICO holds that information relating to a grievance process must not be disclosed by the public authority under the UK Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) since the information is protected by data protection law.

The APD/GBA (the Belgian DPA) found that a hospital that requested an audit by an external expert was the controller for the audit-related processing activity, based on Article 4(7) GDPR. The APD/GBA ordered the hospital to provide access to parts of an audit report based on the right of access, rejecting (for lack of evidence) the exceptions invoked by the hospital (confidentiality, IP rights, personal data of others).
ICO decides that name-redacted application forms must not be disclosed by the public authority under UK Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA), since they are protected by data protection law.

The Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia issued an opinion regarding the conduct of employers towards their employees in the context of testing for the spread of coronavirus. It was held that an employer must take a holistic approach to defining which measures to put in place to curb the spread of the virus, which could include asking their employees to get tested, and in some instances, asking for the results of their test. However, it was held that employers could not require that their employees tell them which countries they will be visiting on their annual leave.

A housing cooperative had incorrectly judged that the use of an electric lock system did not process personal data. The Finnish DPA ruled that, as individuals could be indirectly identified, the housing cooperative had acted unlawfully and ordered to bring the data processing activities in line with GDPR.

In the context of an investigation against SPARTOO SAS, a company specialised in online footwear shopping with activities in thirteen EU countries, the French DPA (Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés- CNIL), as the lead supervisory authority in cooperation with DPAs from other EU countries held that the processing activities of SPARTOO SAS did not comply with a series of GDPR provisions (art. 5§1(c), 5§1(e), 13, 32 GDPR). In that respect, CNIL imposed a fine of 250,000 euros and called SPARTOO SAS to bring its processing activities in conformity with GDPR in a period of three months since the publication of the decision.

The Danish DPA reported Arp-Hansen Hotel Group A/S to the police and recommended DKK 1.1 million. The district court (Retten i Lyngby) found the company guilty, but the case was settled without a penalty (strafbortfald). The case was appealed, and on 20 September 2023 the Eastern High Court (Østre Landsret) fined the company DKK 1 million. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

A voter complained after receiving a personalised election letter addressed to her as a 'possibly new resident' ahead of the October 2018 municipal elections. The Inspectorate found that the lead candidate and mayor had had candidates strike names from the 2018 voters' list, using personal knowledge and a comparison with the 2012 list, to create a 'new residents list'. The Litigation Chamber held that this processing had no lawful basis under Art. 6(1) and breached purpose limitation. It also held that the letter gave inadequate information under Art. 12 and 14. It issued two reprimands and a fine of EUR 3,000, reduced from the intended EUR 5,000 because the party's spending was limited.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) opined that an employer may ask the place of employees' intended holidays for the purpose of protection against COVID-19 only if this meets the requirements of Article 15(5) ZIUPDV, national law on handling the pandemic.

Weak technical and organizational security measures at Tarom led to the unauthorized access and disclosure of the personal data belonging to five passengers. The National Supervisory Authority imposed a fine of 24,182.50 lei (approx. 5,000 Euros).

The ICO held that the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) was entitled to withhold disclosing one name on a document on the grounds that there was no lawful basis for its disclosure under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and therefore 'processing' the personal data by disclosing the name would breach Article 5(1)(a). Following this line of reasoning, the ICO decided that the DHSC was entitled to rely on Section 40(2) and Section 40(3A) of the Freedom of Information Act to prevent disclosing the name.

The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) issued a fine against Forbes Hungary which published the list of the 50 wealthiest Hungarians and the list of the biggest family-owned businesses, for not performing a balance of interests prior to the publication and lack of information on the rights of the complainant.

A former employee complained to the Hungarian authority that his ex-employer still kept a temporary home address that had ceased in 1999, and that it passed his personal data to a card provider without his consent. The authority found that the employer failed to erase or correct the address, did not reply about the measures taken on the request, and transferred data for the holiday-card (SZÉP) application without proper information or legal basis. It fined the employer HUF 600,000, and ordered HUF 10,000 paid to the complainant for exceeding the procedural deadline. It closed the part of the case asking for an order to keep accurate data.
Finnish DPA held that controller should have acquired data subject's consent before sending direct marketing communications to the data subject's work pone

The Finnish DPA imposed a 7,000 euro fine to a company that sent out direct marketing communications without obtaining prior consent from the data subjects and for also neglecting data subjects’ rights.

Data subject objected to direct marketing as per Article 21 GDPR and requested for their data to be deleted as per Article 17 GDPR. The Finnish DPA held that the controller had not fulfilled their duty in accordance with the articles.

Following an inspection planned by the Czech DPA for 2020, the Office found a company liable for a misdemeanour under the Czech Act 110/2019. From 24 May 2018 to 25 May 2020 its privacy policy, which was meant to give the Articles 12-14 information, sat under the 'Contacts' tab of its website without users being told, so it was hard to find and incomplete. This breached Article 12(1) GDPR. The Office issued a penalty order fining the company CZK 10,000, near the bottom of the range, noting the company corrected the problem during the inspection.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation into the national postal company after it notified a personal data breach. Appropriate technical and organisational measures were not in place to prevent unauthorised access to email addresses and phone numbers on one of its web addresses, compromising the confidentiality of data of 81 people. The company was found to have breached Article 32 GDPR and was fined RON 9,686.60, stated as equivalent to EUR 2,000.

Upon examining the national application "StopCovid", the French data protection authority (CNIL) found that the data processing was not fully compliant with the provisions of the GDPR and the national data protection law.

A company renting ski and sports equipment routinely scanned or copied its customers' ID cards without being able to prove consent, collecting far more data than needed, such as the birth number and ID card number. It also failed to show that it gave customers the Article 13 information and informed them of their Article 15-21 rights. The Office issued a penalty order finding two misdemeanours and imposed a fine of CZK 10,000 under the absorption principle. It also ordered the company to amend its rental contract, delete all ID scans and destroy paper copies within 10 days, and report compliance.

A Belgian resident complained that Google refused to delist search results linking him to a harassment complaint that had been found unfounded in 2010, and to results labelling him as belonging to a political party. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint for results 1 to 8 but found that results 9 to 12 should have been delisted, breaching Articles 17(1)(a) and 6(1)(f) GDPR, and that Google's reply lacked transparent reasoning, breaching Article 12. It ordered delisting and amendment of the online forms, and imposed fines of EUR 500,000 and EUR 100,000. The decision was later annulled by the Market Court on 30 June 2021.

The Norwegian DPA reduced an initial fine to Rælingen municipality from €80,000 to €50,000 related to the use of the school app "Showbie", for lack of sufficient technical and organisational measures for processing special categories of data, cf. Article 32(1)(b) GDPR, Article 32(1)(d), Article 24 and Article 35, cf. Article 5.

Finnish DPA ordered Euroclear Finland Oy to align its data disclosure activities with data protection regulations. Disclosing shareholder register information via the company's telephone service and disclosing information for direct marketing purposes was held to be unlawful.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation on 23 June 2020 into Proleasing Motors SRL after the company notified a personal data breach. During an online contest on its Facebook page, a screenshot of the website source code was posted that included the password to the forms completed by contest participants, giving unauthorised access to the data of 436 customers. The authority found a breach of Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR and fined the company 72,642 lei (about EUR 15,000). It also ordered the company to review and update its technical and organisational measures, including electronic communication procedures.

Merlini s.r.l., an agency selling Wind Tre products, used freelance 'procacciatori' without any written contract or data protection designation. One of them ran an unlawful call centre in Rome holding lists of over 500,000 records, and passed contract proposals and personal data to Merlini without consent or a valid legal basis. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 7, 28 and 29 GDPR and the telemarketing rules. It fined Merlini EUR 200,000, ordered it to bind the procacciatori by contract, banned processing through them until then, and ordered publication of the decision. The case was also sent to the judicial authority.

The Italian DPA examined over 100 files of complaints and reports about Wind Tre's data processing, mainly unwanted promotional contacts, and carried out inspections of Wind Tre and some partners. It found unlawful marketing without valid consent, consent collected through the MyWind and My3 apps in a defective way, insufficient control over the sales chain and partners, failures to honour objections, unauthorised publication of data in telephone directories, and breaches of accountability and privacy by design. It imposed a fine of EUR 16,729,600, equal to 8% of the maximum statutory fine, and ordered a ban on certain processing together with corrective measures within 180 days. It also ordered publication of the decision as an ancillary sanction.

The Italian DPA received complaints and reports about Iliad, a new mobile operator, and carried out an inspection in May 2019. It found problems with how the privacy notice and consent were presented, with the privacy of customers using self-service Simbox SIM activation machines, and with the security of stored telephone traffic data, which an administrator profile could see in clear. For the notice and consent issues it only issued a reprimand, as minor infringements. For the Simbox it reprimanded and ordered corrective measures. For the traffic data it ordered compliance within 120 days and imposed a fine of EUR 800,000, set at 4% of the 20 million maximum.

The Garante received a complaint that the municipality of Baronissi had left online, in the historical section of its official notice board, a municipal urban-planning order containing the personal data of a couple. The data included dates and places of birth, residence, property and cadastral details, information on unauthorised building works and photographs. The document stayed online far longer than the fifteen days allowed, with no legal basis for the excess period, and it contained more data than necessary. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness and data minimisation principles and of Article 6, fined the municipality EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the data had been removed.

A state school in Crucoli published on its website rankings of students applying to a regional (POR Calabria) project. The rankings showed in clear partial scores on school drop-out risk, insufficient grades, ISEE income indicator and disability, including health data of a student. The school said an administrative assistant had published the wrong version by mistake. The Garante found the processing unlawful (Arts 5, 6, 9 GDPR and Italian Code provisions) and fined the school EUR 2,000, ordering publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed since the data had been removed.

An employee complained to the Italian DPA about his employer. The company had deactivated his work email account while he was on sick leave, refused access to the mailbox contents, and a manager had forwarded an email exchange to colleagues. The Garante found that the company had not informed the employee about how the work email would be handled during sick leave, breaching the transparency and fairness requirements. The forwarding complaint was left aside because the Vicenza court had already dealt with it. The Garante ordered the company to give the employee access to the mailbox, possibly with an expert, and fined it EUR 20,000.

The Cypriot Data Protection Authority held that the footage from a CCTV system of an individual shall be handled as subject to Article 4(1) of the GDPR Regulation. The meaning of that conclusion is that the Data Controller is obligated to provide access to the affected individual.

The President of the Personal Data Protection Office (UODO) imposed a fine of 5 000 (approx. 1170 EUR) on an individual entrepreneur running a non-public nursery and pre-school for failure to provide the UODO with access to personal data and other information necessary for the performance of its tasks (Article 58(1)(e) GDPR).

After a complaint against Xfera Móviles, the Spanish DPA sent the company an information request, which it received on 11 November 2019 but never answered. The AEPD opened a penalty procedure for obstructing its investigative powers under Article 58(1) GDPR, proposing a fine of EUR 5,000. The company paid EUR 3,000 on 11 June 2020, using both the 20% reduction for acknowledging responsibility and the 20% reduction for voluntary payment. The AEPD therefore declared the procedure terminated under Article 85 LPACAP.

A former lorry driver complained that his employer, GTL s.r.l., never answered his access request for tachograph records and driver-card data. The company also ignored two requests for information from the Garante, and only said it had forgotten when inspected by the Guardia di Finanza. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR and of Article 157 of the Italian Code. It fined the company EUR 3,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A school posted at the entrance of its nursery school lists with children's names, birth dates, addresses and phone numbers, by mere error. After reports to the Garante, it found the disclosure had no legal basis and breached the lawfulness and data minimisation principles. The health data claim (vaccine note) was not proven. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and fined the school EUR 2,000, ordering publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the lists had been removed.

A woman complained that INPS Brescia had not answered her request for access to her health data. The Garante invited INPS to reply and it did not do so in time. As the access request predated 25 May 2018, the old Code applied and it carried no administrative fine, so that part was closed. The Garante found INPS had breached Art. 157 of the Code by not answering the Garante's request for information, and fined it EUR 5,000 under Art. 83(5)(a) GDPR, with publication of the decision.

A former employee complained that her employer, a supermarket-operating company, posted her dismissal letter with her personal details on the company notice board. The company did not respond to the authority's notice of violations. The Garante found the processing unlawful for lack of a legal basis and breach of the principles of fairness and data minimisation/proportionality. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000, taking into account the company's micro-enterprise accounts and pending bankruptcy proceedings, and ordered publication of the decision.

A municipal employee complained that the extraordinary commission running the municipality of Manduria sent a press note to local and regional newspapers naming her and disclosing her claim for payment for higher-level duties. The Garante found the municipality had no legal basis to disclose her data to the press, since no law provided for it and the transparency rules invoked did not apply. It fined the municipality EUR 2,000, taking into account that only one person was affected, no special categories were involved, and the municipality had asked the newspapers to remove the articles. Publication of the decision on the Garante's website was also ordered.

The Region of Campania published on its institutional website a document containing the names and residence of two people, together with the amount of a debt the Region owed them under an enforceable judgment. The Garante found no legal basis for putting this online and held the publication breached data minimisation. The data stayed online for several years and was only blacked out after the Garante asked for information. The Garante fined the Region EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Polish DPA began an inspection of the Surveyor General's publication of personal data from the land and building register on the GEOPORTAL2 portal. The Surveyor General refused consent to inspection of the main items in the inspectors' authorisations, arguing that a land register number is not personal data. The inspectors could therefore only check security measures and the appointment of a DPO. The DPA opened proceedings of its own motion and found breaches of Articles 31 and 58(1)(e) and (f) GDPR (failure to cooperate and to give access). It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 100,000, the maximum for a public finance sector body.

A former employee complained that his company e-mail account was kept active after his employment ended on 31 July 2017, with incoming messages automatically forwarded to his former superior for over ten months, and that his access and erasure requests were not answered in time. The Garante found that the company had not informed the employee of this practice, had accessed 238 messages including personal content, and had answered the rights requests only after the Authority intervened. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), (c), (e), 12, 13 and 15 GDPR. It ordered the company to bring its handling of data subject requests into line with Article 12, fined it EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The ICO imposed a fine of £90.000 against on Decision Technologies Limited ('DTL') for a breach of Regulation 22 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, which, except under certain circumstances, did not permit the transmission of unsolicited emails to the subscribers for marketing purposes without specific consent for it, even with the support of third parties ('indirect marketing').

Belgium DPA looked into the complaint of a person whose Facebook profile picture was shared by the defendant by email without his consent. The organization that shared the picture was looking to comply with the prior judgement of the Sports Court prohibiting the complainant from attending training sessions, championships or other competitions organized by one defendant. Belgium DPA decided that this kind of processing was allowed under the legal basis of legitimate interest of the controller.

Fine set by the district court (byretten). The Danish DPA reported Lejre Municipality to the police and recommended DKK 50,000. The municipality was fined DKK 50,000. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

The ICO rejected a request made by the Cheltenham Flood and Drainage Panel (the 'complainant') to the Gloucestershire County Council (the 'Council') in order to disclose some information regarding the staffing and resourcing allocated to the Lead Local Flood Authority (the 'LLFA'). In particular, the disclosure of the data would have been unlawful, due to the fact that there was insufficient legitimate interest to outweigh the data subjects’ fundamental rights and freedoms.

The President of the Personal Data Protection Office (UODO) imposed a penalty of a reprimand for the processing of students’ personal data without legal basis in connection with survey carried out by a school in the school year 2019/2020.

The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) fined private college € 5.000 because it failed to prove the lawfulness of data processing with regard to phone offers of seminars to unemployed people. The college violated the principles of lawfulness of processing and accountability.
The Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA) fined politician € 2.500 for sending unsolicited political SMSs to people without their consent.

The Austrian DPA holds that making by the post office a copy of a recipient's identity card does not infringe complainant's right to privacy and the post office has a legitimate interest in processing the personal data contained in the identity document to safeguard or defend its legal claims.

The Baden-Württemberg data protection authority fined the statutory health insurer AOK Baden-Württemberg EUR 1,240,000 by decision of 25 June 2020. Between 2015 and 2019 the AOK ran prize draws and collected participants' personal data, intending to use it for advertising only with consent. Its technical and organisational measures were insufficient, so data of more than 500 participants was used for advertising without consent. The fine took into account the AOK's cooperation and internal improvements, as well as its size and its public role in the health system, including the strain of the Corona pandemic. Insured persons' data was not affected.
The Persónuvernd (Icelandic DPA) held that a bank's planned publication of photographs including children on its Facebook page was not in compliance with the GDPR.
The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) rejected a complaint where an individual argued that their medical records were unlawfully processed in a dispute over the settlement of benefits.

GBA found that the use of personal data obtained from the national data-bank of vehicles by insurance companies for the purpose of creating personalized price offers constitutes violation of Articles 5, 6, 12, 13 and 14 of GDPR. The agency that maintains this data base, the Federal Public Service Mobility and Transportation, was ordered to bring its data processing in compliance with Articles 5 and 6 within 6 months and Articles 12, 13 and 14 within 3 months. GBA has also issued a reprimand for the violation of Articles 12-14. No fines were issued because the predecessor of GBA had reviewed and issued conditions under which this processing could be approved back in 2017 under the previous data protection law.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) held that the online publication of an Ombudsman's opinion containing the unredacted name and personal details of an individual was a breach of Articles 5 and 6 of the GDPR.

The APD/GBA (Belgian DPA) fined a controller 10,000 EUR for continuing to send a complainant marketing emails after he requested they stop, and for failing to fulfil the complaint's right to access information about the processing by the controller.

The Cyprus DPA held that the inability of the data controller to discover the original contract with the data subject constitutes a violation of the right to access the personal data. A fine of € 15000 was issued.

The APD/GBA (the Belgian DPA) found that a schoolboard violated the data minimisation and transparency principles of the GDPR, and processed data unlawfully by submitting a detailed "wellbeing" survey to a group of 12 year old pupils at a school without obtaining the consent of their parents.

A staff member of PVV Overijssel emailed an invitation to 101 recipients with all email addresses visible to everyone. Because the recipients were supporters, the addresses revealed political opinions, a special category of data. The Dutch DPA found this was a personal data breach that PVV Overijssel never reported to it, in breach of Article 33(1) GDPR. The base fine of EUR 525,000 was cut to EUR 7,500 because the foundation has limited financial capacity.

The ICO rules that The Queen’s interests and rights override the public- legitimate interests in confirming or denying whether the Cabinet Office has information about the exchanged correspondance between The Queen and the PM.

The Spanish data protection authority ('AEPD') issued a resolution against Xfera Móviles S.A. with a fine of €75,000 for sending communication to the complainant who was not a client of the company since 2017.

The DSB helds that, there is therefore no violation of the right to secrecy, as the transmission of health data can be based on § 11a (1) item 3 and (2) item 2 VersVG and the complainant has an obligation to provide information and evidence to the respondent on the basis of the clear order in § 34 VersVG.

Datatilsynet issued the controller Folkehelseinstituttet (the Institute of Public Health) a temporary ban on the processing of personal data by the covid-19 tracking app “Smittestopp”. Datatilsynet found a breach of the principle of data minimization, the right of access and the principle of transparency, pursuant to Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(c) and 15.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that publishes personal data of individuals (names, birth dates, business and insolvency information) on its website. Several people objected and asked for erasure between 2019 and 2020, but the company never erased the data and ignored the authority's call to remedy the situation. The authority found a breach of the right to erasure under Article 17(1) GDPR and fined the company CZK 100,000. Aggravating factors were the long duration, multiple data subjects, no remedy after the warning, and a previous fine.

UniCredit notified the Garante in July 2017 of an intrusion, between April 2016 and July 2017, that gave unauthorised access to data of about 762,000 people through the Speedy Arena application, using credentials of staff of an external partner. The Garante found weak authorisation profiles, inadequate and wrongly retained tracking logs, no alerts and no internal audits. The case was decided under the old Italian Privacy Code (not the GDPR). It fined the bank EUR 600,000 in total, made up of three separate fines, and rejected the bank's defence that the partner's misuse of credentials and a software bug excused it.

Greek DPA holds that the use of unsolicited electronic communications for the purposes of direct marketing for the promotion of the defendant's candidacy at the parliament elections of 2019 violated Article 13 of the ePrivacy Directive.
The Spanish DPA fined Equifax, a credit agency, €75,000 for unlawful processing of data.

A former public employee of a university asked for access to the archived 2018 emails of his work mailbox after his employment ended; the university refused, citing data protection. The authority found the refusal unlawful as regards private emails, and found that the university failed to give transparent information on the action taken on the request. It ordered the university to review, with the complainant, which emails are private and to give access to them, rejected the request for work-related emails, and imposed a fine of HUF 200,000. It also ordered HUF 10,000 paid to the complainant for exceeding the procedural deadline.

The Personuvernd (Icelandic DPA) stated in an opinion that exchanges of personal data of foreign prisoners between state agencies (in this case, between the Immigration Office and the Prison and Probation Service) was permissible, provided that the exchange is necessary for the agencies to carry out their legal obligations and that the agencies ensured a sufficient level of security of the data preventing any unauthorised access.

A sole trader running a non-public nursery and pre-school notified a personal data breach in June 2019, after people entered the premises and changed the locks. The Polish DPA repeatedly asked for an anonymised copy of the notice sent to data subjects, to check Article 34 compliance. The controller did not collect most of the letters and did not answer the one it received. The DPA found a breach of Article 58(1)(e) and imposed a fine of PLN 5,000 (stated as EUR 1,168), using an estimated company size because no financial data was provided. The decision is final.
The DPA ordered Google to remove several links from Google Search concerning a data subject's arrest warrant, as this information was outdated and was no longer of importance to society.

The Cypriot Comissioner ordered video game company to bring its processing operations into compliance with Article 12(2) GDPR as it found they should implement additional modalities to facilitate data subjects' rights and enable the latter to justify their identity according to Article 12(6) GDPR.

The Garante per la protezione dei dati personali has authorised the Ministry of Health to initiate the processing of the Covid-19 alert system (through the app "Immuni"). The Garante has, however, decided to impose a series of further measures aimed at strengthening the security of the processing.

Belgian DPA (Litigation Chamber) imposed a fine of € 1000 on a non-profit organisation for direct marketing practices without legal basis and notwithstanding the repeated objections to the processing by the complainant.

The Finnish DPA (Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto) fined Taksi Helsinki € 72,000 for failing to assess the risks and effects of personal data processing before adopting a camera surveillance system that records audio and video in its taxis.

The President of the Personal Data Protection Office (UODO) imposed a fine of 15 000 PLN (approx. 3500 EUR) on East Power company from Jelenia Góra for failing to provide the supervisory authority with access to personal data and other information necessary for the performance of its tasks. The Polish DPA found that the company violated Art 58(1)(e) GDPR.

The Austrian DPA ordered a bank to delete a copy of the data subject's driver's license it had retained to comply with the Austrian Financial Markets Money Laundering Act; the bank was not required to verify the data subject's identity under the law.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) held that banks are entitled to have access to information on a data subjects' domicile, on the basis that the banks have a legitimate interest to process such personal data.

The Icelandic DPA decided that the processing of the Complainant's personal data by Creditinfo Lánstraust hf. in connection with the preparation of a credit report within the four-year period was in compliance with the Icelandic Act no. 90/2018 on Data Protection and the Processing of Personal Data, and did not violate Article 5 GDPR.

The Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL) delivered its opinion on the Draft Decree relating to the "StopCovid" app and provided some specific comments on the conditions of its implementation in the light of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It welcomed the temporary and voluntary character of the app and provided some recommendations in order for the app to be more privacy friendly. The final version of the Decree having regard on this deliberation is décret n° 2020-650 du 29 mai 2020.

A patient, after her hospitalisation thought that a detailed medical report is part of her personal data which have been collected by the Hospital, and for that reason, claimed that she shall receive the medical report under the veil of GDPR. The Cypriot Office of the Commissioner for Personal Data Protection disagreed.

The Austrian Data Protection Authority (DSB) held (for the second time) that a legal person has the constitutional right to data protection under § 1 DSG (Austrian Data Protection Act) and is entitled to lodge a complaint before the DSB.

The Italian DPA issued a favourable opinion on the draft decree of the president of the Council of State laying down the technical rules for the implementation of the electronic administrative proceedings from May 30 to July 31, 2020, due to the Covid-19 emergency.

In a non-binding opinion, the Slovenian DPA (IP), stated that its National Institute of Public Health (NIJZ) could use data from its infectious database to invite COVID-19 survivors to participate in another body's treatment and research trials which involved the collection of their data.

This is an Irish Times news article, not the decision itself. It reports that Tusla was fined €75,000 by the Data Protection Commission after an investigation into three cases in which information about children was wrongly disclosed to unauthorised parties. In one case a mother's and child's contact and location data went to an alleged abuser; in two foster-care cases data went to blood relatives, including an imprisoned father. The fine was confirmed by a Circuit Court filing, and Tusla did not intend to contest it.

No fine. The Danish DPA reported JobTeam A/S to the police and recommended DKK 50,000; the district court acquitted the company. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.
The litigation chamber concluded that the "invite a friend" function of a social media platform violates the GDPR since consent from the users was not collected.

INPS notified the Garante of two personal data breaches that occurred around 31 March to 2 April 2020, when many users tried to access its portal for COVID-19 benefits. The first was a misconfigured CDN cache that let some users see other people's registry data; the second was a flaw in the Bonus Baby Sitting application procedure that let unauthorised users view, change, delete or submit other users' applications concerning minors. The Garante ordered INPS under Article 58(2)(e) to notify all affected data subjects without delay and within 15 days, and asked for documented proof within 20 days. No fine was imposed; the Garante reserved the right to take further, including sanctioning, measures once the investigation is complete.
The Icelandic DPA decided that an alleged sending of an email, whose existence is not proven in the course of a complaint, does not fall within the material scope of Article 2(1) GDPR.

The Swedish DPA fined a Health and Medical Committee about €11,350 (SEK 120,000) for publishing sensitive personal data of a patient on a webpage without a legal basis. The DPA further ruled that instead of orally instructions written ones are needed for the publication on the webpage.

Following a personal data breach, the Belgian DPA assessed whether the controller had violated Articles 5, 24, 28, 33 and 34 GDPR, however they found that none of these provisions were breached by the controller.
The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) fined Banca Comercială Română S.A. 5,000 € for failing to implement adequate technical and organisational measures when processing personal data of adults and minors.

After a typing error during changes in clients' information, a client had access to another client's data through the web-banking platform. The DPA negotiated the role of data management procedures of a bank, under the aegis of GDPR.

The Estonian DPA (AKI) ordered an apartment association to cease the disclosure of photos depicting members of the association in places where third parties had access, without obtaining prior consent. It also imposed € 500 fine as injunction.
Belgium's DPA reasserts the principle of accountability in accordance article 24 GDPR and the necessity of documenting all processes and procedures resulting thereof.
The Litigation Chamber of the Belgian DPA imposed a €50,000 fine on a company for non-compliance with the requirements relating to the appointment and function of a DPO under the GDPR.

The Romanian supervisory authority completed an investigation into Telekom Romania Communications SA on 23 April 2020. A complainant said contracts had been fraudulently concluded in his name. The authority found the company lacked sufficient security measures, in particular checks on the accuracy of personal data collected by phone, so new subscription contracts were made using data from an existing contract without verification, breaching Article 32 GDPR. The company was fined 14,524.2 lei (stated as EUR 3,000) and ordered to put in place effective identification procedures, regular staff training and periodic compliance checks.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) opined that an insurance company is entitled to ask personal data when it is necessary to justify an insurance claim but it could not assess if this would be necessary and proportionate for information dated five years ago.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued the non-binding opinion that the personal data of researchers employed by a public institute is in principle not personal data but publicly available information. However, a concrete assessment about the nature of this and the legal basis has to be made by the data controller.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion about apps which would track the state of health and the movements of confirmed patients with SARS-CoV-2. The IP opined that a DPIA would be mandatory and that EU member states should coordinate their actions regarding such apps.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion about employees' personal data that an employer can process during work from home. The IP emphasised that the principles of data minimisation and transparency must be respected as well as the information obligations according to Articles 13 and 14 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA finds that videosurveillance is a processing likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms and that a data controller that employs fewer than 250 persons is therefore still subject to Article 30(1) GDPR in this regard, having to establish a record of processing activities for videosurveillance.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion regarding the processing of personal data of teachers and pupils when new technologies are used in order to offer or participate in a lesson. The IP opined that data controllers (i.e. schools) should seek for an adequate legal basis and pay attention in particular to their information obligation, the security of personal data, possible data transfers to the US and the principle of data minimisation.

The Bulgarian DPA fined a political party about €1000 (BGN 2000) for processing personal data without a legal ground as required by Article 6(1) GDPR, after hiring a handwriting expert to determine that an alleged signature was fake.

On April 14, 2020, the ICO supported the decision of the Insolvency Service to withold the information it held about insolvent companies. Furthermore, it stated that the confirmation or denial by the Insolvency Serivce that it held more information about the companies within the scope of the request invovled the disclosure of personal data itself.

The Slovenian Data Protection Authority (IP) issued an advisory opinion on the lawfulness of a telephone application which would track individuals for the containment of the COVID-19 spread. The IP stressed that any such solution should respect the Constitution, the GDPR, the the Electronic Communications Act (ZEKom-1) and the Data Protection Act (ZVOP-1) and its effectiveness should be assessed in advance.

The HDPA issued an opinion requested by the Supreme Council For Civil Personnel Selection (ASEP) on the basis of Article 36 GDPR regarding the online publication of tables with the ranking and the appointment of candidates for civil service positions.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion under Article 58(3) GDPR regarding the lawfulness of processing of a photograph. The IP clarified that a photograph can be considered personal data, especially when a photo depicts an individual clearly and unambiguously allowing for their identification. Such processing must be based on a consent under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR collected in advance of such processing.

Category:Article 4(1) GDPR Category:2019 The President of the Personal Data Protection Office in Poland (PUODO) decided to discontinue proceedings concerning the processing of data in connection with the requirement for Polish judges and prosecutors to submit declarations about their membership in associations. The PUODO clarified that the obligation to submit the above mentioned statements clearly results from the provisions of the national law and thus falls under one of the legal grounds in Article 6(1)(c) GDPR. The President of the Personal Data Protection Office (UODO) stated that he cannot make a decision regarding the constitutionality of such an obligation providing that this is a competence of the Constitutional Tribunal. The Ombudsman has the right to submit motions on the compliance of acts with the Polish Constitution to the Constitutional Tribunal.
The AEPD fined a controller for not providing its users with complete information regarding the use of cookies.

The Information Commissioner’s Office of the UK (ICO) found that a full disclosure of information requested by data subject relating to data analysis reports produced for the Pay Consistency Panel and pay progression assessments would violate Section 40 FOIA and Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. A three-step test was carried out to assess the lawfulness.

The IP issued the opinion that the police, when performing their tasks, may lawfully access video footage without the participants' consent, while any third party, such as an insurance company, should have an adequate legal basis under Article 6 GDPR to lawfully do so.

The Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA) issued a reprimand to AXA Insurance because it failed to fulfill the right to erasure of personal data collected at the pre-contractual stage. The HDPA reserved its judgement on the lawfulness of the draft Code of Conduct of the Insurance Companies' Association, as requested according to Article 40(5) GDPR, with regard to the five-year retention period of personal data collected at the pre-contractual stage which is foreseen for the prevention of and fight against insurance fraud.

A dismissed employee complained that her employer had accessed the browsing history of her work PC, using a password shared with the company's legal representative, and used it in disciplinary proceedings ending in dismissal. The Garante found that the company gave no adequate prior information on monitoring, shared passwords contrary to security requirements, relied on a vague internal policy on internet checks, and only partly answered the access request without valid reasons. It ordered a restriction of the browsing-history data to storage for legal defence, compliance with the access request, security and policy changes, and fined the company EUR 10,000.
The AEPD fined mobile network operator Xfera Móviles, S.A.U. EUR. 5,000 because it failed to comply with the AEPD's order to provide all necessary information as required in Article 58(1) GDPR.

A data subject lodged a complaint against the Norwegian DPA alleging several GDPR violations. A third party was appointed to handle the case, since the DPA itself cannot handle complaints filed against it. The appointed representative held that the DPA violated Article 13 GDPR for failing to specify the legitimate interests for processing personal data on their website.

The Dutch DPA received a tip that CP&A, an inspection and maintenance company, kept an online sickness-absence register with health data of its employees. The register was a Google Drive file and it covered 25 sick employees. Between 12 March and 2 May 2019 the AP visited the web address known to it six times and found that it could view the register without any authentication or other access control. CP&A said the file could be reached only through a specific link, given to the people who handled sick leave and re-integration; the AP still found the security inadequate. The AP found a breach of the ban on processing health data (Art. 9(1) GDPR) and of the security obligation (Art. 32(1) GDPR). Policy rules produced base fines of EUR 725,000 and EUR 310,000 (EUR 1,035,000 together), but because CP&A's financial capacity is limited the AP reduced the total to EUR 15,000.

The Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante) delivered an opinion stating that the Udine City Council acted lawfully when providing for a limited civic access to the minutes of a district council meeting. The Garante considered the disclosure of the full handwritten minutes would have been unlawful, since violating the principles of purpose limitation and data minimization under Article 5(1)(b) and (c) GDPR.

The Information commission (the IP) issued an opinion explaining in which situation it is necessary for an employer to obtain information on employee’s sick leave for supervisory purposes, under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.

The HDPA fined € 5.000 private centre for speech therapy because it did not fulfill the right of access exercised by a parent, who had the parental responsibility but not the custody, on behalf of his minor child. The controller also ignored HDPA's previous order to comply with the parent's request, thus violating Article 15(1) and (4) GDPR as well as the principle of accountability pursuant to Article 5(2) GDPR.

Category:Article 58(3) GDPR The Slovenian Supervisory Authority (IP) issued an opinion as foreseen under Article 58(3) GDPR on the issue of the health data sharing under Article 9 GDPR in the employer - employee context. It held that there is no reason to collect such data by all organisations and companies, since in principle such information is provided through the National Institute of Public Health (NIJZ) epidemiological service. For all the other cases, the respective exceptions under Article 9(2) GDPR may apply.

Category:Article 58(3) GDPR The Slovenian Supervisory Authority (IP) issued an opinion as foreseen under Article 58(3) GDPR on the issue of the validity of consent to access digital content and online classrooms during the state of emergency in the Slovenia. The IP found that the consent may be given in writing, electronically or in another appropriate manner, and in any case should fulfill the requirements under Article 7 and Article 8 GDPR.

The Spanish data protection authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of 6,000 EUR on Oliveros Ustrell because the company could not prove the existence of consent for data processing activities, including the transfer of data to Vodafone.

A man who said he was assaulted at a bar asked the controller to freeze and later give him access to its camera footage, but received no proper answers, and the footage was deleted after 30 days without telling him. The Authority partly upheld his complaint, finding the controller failed to inform him properly about his restriction, access and footage requests, and ordered it to fulfil the access request. It also found, ex officio, a breach of the accountability principle in the camera surveillance. It fined the controller HUF 2,000,000 and rejected the complainant's own request for a fine.
